subject: Tenant traffic contracts and gateway expectations for private deploy

Subject: Tenant traffic contracts and gateway expectations for private deploy

Hi Chloe,

Thanks again for the demo last week. We're starting the network readiness work on our side for the private Redwood deployment and have a couple of ask items to align on before we hand the ticket to infra: 

- Do you have an expected list of source/destination CIDRs and ports for control plane vs inference traffic? We want to ensure our NGFW rules don't accidentally block the control plane heartbeats.
- How does Redwood expect to terminate TLS for data-plane requests inside our VPC? Is mutual TLS required between inference workers and customer-side ingress? Or is a fronting TLS termination at our edge acceptable with mTLS to Redwood?
- Can you confirm whether the control plane uses outbound-only connections (redwood-managed endpoints) or if we need to accept inbound connections from Redwood IP ranges?
- Any constraints on per-tenant bandwidth shaping or egress NAT behavior we should model?

If you have a short reference doc or a sample policy we can use, that would speed things up. We'd like to finalize firewall and NAT rules by EOD next Tues.

Thanks,

Sara Long
Network Eng - ACME Corp

On Thu, Sep 3, 2026 at 10:12 AM Sara Long <sara.long@acme.com> wrote:
> Thanks again for the demo last week...

Hi Sara — thanks for the clear list. I've attached a short draft (tenant-egress-contracts-draft.pdf) that contains the concrete CIDR/port tables and the recommended NAT/egress model. High level answers below, followed by action items for infra: 

1) Control plane vs data plane CIDRs and ports
- Control plane (management/heartbeat): outbound HTTPS to our control endpoints: 443/TCP to api.redwood-managed.net (we list the expected IP blocks in the attached sample). Keep outbound allowed from the management subnet.
- Data plane (inference connections): typically TLS-terminated at customer edge and proxied to workers on ephemeral ports. Recommended: allow 1024-65535/TCP for worker egress if you plan to NAT; otherwise we can negotiate fixed ports during handoff.

2) TLS termination
- Our preferred model: mutual TLS between Redwood inference workers and the customer ingress for inter-worker data-plane trust. However, we support an alternate model where your edge performs TLS termination and we establish an mTLS session from edge -> Redwood workers (so long as certificate validation and client auth are preserved).

3) Control plane connectivity model
- Control plane is outbound-only from customer VPC to Redwood control endpoints by default. No inbound firewall holes are required. We do publish a set of IP ranges for customers who must whitelist. If you require inbound from Redwood (rare), we can coordinate but it requires a peering/port-open process.

4) Bandwidth shaping and egress NAT
- Redwood does not require a specific NAT behavior, but note: per-tenant egress accounting is easiest when you preserve source IPs or use a consistent SNAT mapping per worker pool. If you SNAT all tenants to a single IP, we'll need to rely on application-level tagging for billing/metrics. For bandwidth shaping, we recommend policing at edge with the following profiles:
  * baseline inference: 50 Mbps per tenant
  * heavy inference (batch): configurable; suggest burst policy to 500 Mbps for short windows

Action items (proposal):
- ACME: Apply attached draft CIDR+ports to staging NGFW and send results by Mon 9/6.
- Redwood (Chloe): share a controlplane-endpoint-sample.txt (attached) with exact IP prefixes and cert fingerprint expected.
- Redwood (Irene): schedule a 30m handoff with your infra to validate NAT behavior and sample flows.

Attachments: tenant-egress-contracts-draft.pdf (table + diagrams), controlplane-endpoint-sample.txt

Best,
Chloe Martin

Adding a couple of operational notes from the serving/runtime side — copying infra runbook link for context: https://redwood-internal.atlassian.net/browse/INF-1123

- If ACME intends to do per-tenant SNAT (one IP per tenant), great — that lets us map metrics and enforce per-tenant QoS more transparently. If SNAT pools are dynamic, please let us know the allocation model so we can align the accounting tags.
- For high-throughput tenants: consider placing them on their own worker pool and route via a dedicated NAT gateway to avoid noisy-neighbor shaping. We can auto-suggest pool sizing once we have expected RPS and average token sizes.
- A quick packet capture (one minute) from a staging run would help verify our header-preservation and TLS behavior; if ACME can provide pcap + timestamps we can validate end-to-end.

I'll be on the handoff call and can run through the worker-pool sizing checklist.

- Aditya
